title: Problem 01
markdown:
### Problem
Let $S_n$ be the sum of the squares of the first $n$ positive odd integers. Find, with proof, the units digit (in base 10) of $S_{2011}$.

### Solution (adapted from the official solution)
The units digit of $S_{2011}$ is 1.

We show this by observing that $S_1 = 1$ has units digit 1, and that $S_{n+10}$ always has the same units digit as does $S_n$.

Modulo 10, the sequence of squares of positive odd integers begins $(1, 9, 5, 9, 1)$, after which this cycle repeats itself, because $(n + 10)^2 = n^2 + 20n + 100 \equiv n^2 \pmod{10}$.

Then modulo 10, $S_{n+10} - S_n$ will always be the sum of 10 consecutive terms in this sequence, which will be

$$1 + 9 + 5 + 9 + 1 + 1 + 9 + 5 + 9 + 1 = 40 \equiv 0 \pmod{10},$$

wherever in the sequence one begins. Thus $S_{n+10} \equiv S_n \pmod{10}$.

Since $2011 \equiv 1 \pmod{10}$, $S_{2011} \equiv S_1 = 1^2 = 1 \pmod{10}$.

### Conceptual Explanation
The sequence of odd squares mod 10 repeats with period 5: $1^2 \equiv 1, 3^2 \equiv 9, 5^2 \equiv 5, 7^2 \equiv 9, 9^2 \equiv 1$. The sum of two full cycles (10 terms) is $2(1 + 9 + 5 + 9 + 1) = 40 \equiv 0 \pmod{10}$. Hence $S_n \pmod{10}$ has period 10, and $S_{2011} \equiv S_1 = 1 \pmod{10}$.

### Key Technique
Periodicity of polynomial sums modulo 10; summing full cycles to establish vanishing offsets.
